claim: Malaria had an estimated 216 million new cases and 445,000 deaths in 2016.
source: Malaria remains a major global health challenge with an estimated 216 million new cases and 445,000 deaths in 2016 (World Health Organization, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to World Health Organization, 2017

claim: New tools will be needed to achieve malaria elimination.
source: Whilst current tools have substantially reduced the global burden of disease, new tools will be needed to achieve malaria elimination (Walker et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Walker et al., 2016

claim: RTS,S/AS01 is the first malaria vaccine to complete Phase III trials.
source: The first malaria vaccine RTS,S/AS01 to complete Phase III trials is a PEV vaccine and has been demonstrated to be partially effective, reducing clinical incidence in 5 – 17-month-old children by 36.3% (95%CI: 31.8 – 40.5%) over 40 months follow-up (RTSS Clinical Trials Partnership, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to RTSS Clinical Trials Partnership, 2015

claim: RTS,S/AS01 reduced clinical incidence in 5-17-month-old children by 36.3% (95%CI: 31.8-40.5%) over 40 months follow-up.
source: The first malaria vaccine RTS,S/AS01 to complete Phase III trials is a PEV vaccine and has been demonstrated to be partially effective, reducing clinical incidence in 5 – 17-month-old children by 36.3% (95%CI: 31.8 – 40.5%) over 40 months follow-up (RTSS Clinical Trials Partnership, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to RTSS Clinical Trials Partnership, 2015 providing clinical trial data

claim: Multiple antigens (e.g. Pfs25, P230, P48/45) have been identified as targets for TBV candidates that can reduce transmission to mosquitoes.
source: Pre-clinical investigations have identified multiple antigens (e.g. Pfs25, P230, P48/45) as targets for TBV candidates that, when administered, can reduce transmission to mosquitoes (Hoffman et al., 2015; Sauerwein and Richie, 2015), but complete, or reproducible, translation to the clinic has not been achieved so far (Talaat et al., 2016; Hoffman et al., 2015; Sauerwein and Richie, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hoffman et al., 2015 and Sauerwein and Richie, 2015

claim: Complete or reproducible translation of TBV candidates to the clinic has not been achieved.
source: Pre-clinical investigations have identified multiple antigens (e.g. Pfs25, P230, P48/45) as targets for TBV candidates that, when administered, can reduce transmission to mosquitoes (Hoffman et al., 2015; Sauerwein and Richie, 2015), but complete, or reproducible, translation to the clinic has not been achieved so far (Talaat et al., 2016; Hoffman et al., 2015; Sauerwein and Richie, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Talaat et al., 2016; Hoffman et al., 2015; Sauerwein and Richie, 2015

claim: Partial protection of PEV malaria vaccines may be due to the over-dispersed distribution of sporozoites in each infectious bite.
source: It has been hypothesized that this may be in part due to the over-dispersed distribution of sporozoites in each infectious bite, such that despite inducing a high per-parasite killing efficacy, the probability that at least one parasite reaches the liver and progresses to blood-stage infection remains high (White et al., 2013; Bejon et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to White et al., 2013 and Bejon et al., 2005

claim: TBVs reduce ookinete and sporozoite density.
source: TBVs have been demonstrated to act in this way, reducing ookinete and sporozoite density (Bompard et al., 2017; Blagborough et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bompard et al., 2017 and Blagborough et al., 2013

claim: mAb-3D11 targets the same corresponding parasite circumsporozoite protein (CSP) as RTS,S.
source: To simulate the antibody response to a PEV, a monoclonal antibody (mAb-3D11) - which targets the same corresponding parasite circumsporozoite protein (CSP) as RTS,S – was passively transferred (intravenously) into mice.
evidence: Direct statement about the antibody target

claim: mAb-3D11 at the selected dose reduces mosquito-to-mouse transmission probability by approximately 50%.
source: To act as a partially effective PEV (broadly comparable to RTS,S), a mAb-3D11 dose was selected which reduces mosquito-to-mouse transmission probability by ~50% (as evaluated in naive mouse populations, transfused with differing doses of 3D11, challenged with five mosquito bites, see Materials and methods).
evidence: Based on experimental evaluation described in Materials and methods

claim: Sterilizing immunity of 47.2% was titrated over multiple challenges for mAb-3D11.
source: Sterilizing immunity of 47.2% was titrated over multiple challenges.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental result

claim: mAb-4B7 targets the same parasite stages as the most currently advanced human TBV candidate, Pfs25.
source: The complementary actions of a TBV antibody response were simulated using an anti-Pfs25 monoclonal antibody 4B7 (mAb-4B7), administered by passive transfer, which targets the same parasite stages as the most currently advanced human TBV candidate, Pfs25 (Talaat et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Talaat et al., 2016

claim: PbPfs25DR3 is phenotypically indistinguishable from WT P. berghei.
source: PbPfs25DR3 is phenotypically indistinguishable to WT P. berghei, expresses Pfs25 on the surface of the zygote/ookinete, and has been used previously to assay a range of TBVs (Goodman et al., 2011; Kapulu et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Goodman et al., 2011 and Kapulu et al., 2015

claim: PbPfs25DR3 expresses Pfs25 on the surface of the zygote/ookinete.
source: PbPfs25DR3 is phenotypically indistinguishable to WT P. berghei, expresses Pfs25 on the surface of the zygote/ookinete, and has been used previously to assay a range of TBVs (Goodman et al., 2011; Kapulu et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Goodman et al., 2011 and Kapulu et al., 2015

claim: At lower TBV antibody dose exposure levels (50% and 65%), the probability of eliminating all parasites from the mouse/mosquito populations was greater when PEV and TBV antibodies were administered together compared to singly.
source: At lower TBV antibody dose exposure levels (50% and 65%), the probability of eliminating all parasites from the mouse/mosquito populations was greater when PEV and TBV antibodies were administered together compared to singly, irrespective of the dose of the TBV antibody administered (Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1

claim: PEV antibody alone reduced the prevalence of infection by 48.0% (95% CrI 36.6-58.0%).
source: we estimated PEV antibody alone to reduce the prevalence of infection by 48.0% (95% credible interval, CrI, 36.6–58.0%).
evidence: Statistical estimate from density model analysis of experimental data

claim: TBV antibody alone reduced the prevalence of infection by 33.9% (95% CrI: 18.2-47.4%), 74.3% (65.7%-82.4%) and 95.8% (90.2%-100%) for the 50%, 65% and 85% individual efficacy titres, respectively.
source: Similarly, use of TBV antibody alone reduced the prevalence of infection by 33.9% (95% CrI: 18.2–47.4%), 74.3% (65.7%–82.4%) and 95.8% (90.2%–100%) for the 50%, 65% and 85% individual efficacy titres, respectively.
evidence: Statistical estimates from density model analysis of experimental data

claim: If the actions of the two antibody types were to act independently, the predicted combined efficacy would be 83.3% (79.1-87.0%).
source: If the actions of the two antibody types were to act independently, the predicted combined efficacy would be 83.3% (79.1–87.0%).
evidence: Statistical inference from model predictions

claim: A substantially higher efficacy of 90.8% (86.7-94.2%) (p=0.0035) was observed in the PEV+TBV antibody group, indicating a synergistic interaction.
source: A substantially higher efficacy of 90.8% (86.7–94.2%) (p=0.0035) was observed in the PEV +TBV antibody group, indicating a synergistic interaction (Table 1).
evidence: Statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Table 1

claim: The 95% Credible Intervals did not overlap the median estimates, demonstrating a significant difference between the two treatments.
source: Here, the 95% Credible Intervals did not overlap the median estimates, demonstrating a significant difference between the two treatments.
evidence: Statistical inference from credible interval analysis

claim: The same synergistic relationship was observed when examining vaccine efficacy against parasite density (p=0.0025).
source: The same relationship was observed when examining vaccine efficacy against parasite density (p=0.0025) (Table 1).
evidence: Statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Table 1

claim: The greatest synergistic enhancement in efficacy against parasite prevalence was seen at lower doses of functional TBV antibodies.
source: Sub-dividing the data by TBV antibody dose, the greatest synergistic enhancement in efficacy against parasite prevalence was seen at lower doses of functional TBV antibodies (Figure 2).
evidence: Analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2

claim: A TBV antibody dose which reduces mouse-to-mosquito transmission by 50% increased the efficacy of PEV antibody prevalence to 82.2% (74.6-88.9%) compared to an expected 65% (57.7-73.2%) efficacy if the vaccines acted independently (p=0.0015).
source: A TBV antibody dose which reduces mouse-to-mosquito transmission by 50% increased the efficacy of PEV antibody prevalence to 82.2% (74.6–88.9%) compared to an expected 65% (57.7–73.2%) efficacy if the vaccines acted independently, a strong indication of synergy (p=0.0015).
evidence: Statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: Weaker synergistic effects were observed against parasite prevalence and density for the PEV+TBV antibody at the 65% dose (p=0.0675, 0.02, respectively).
source: Weaker synergistic effects were observed against parasite prevalence and density for the PEV +TBV antibody at the 65% dose (Figure 2, p=0.0675, 0.02, respectively) (Table 1).
evidence: Statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2 and Table 1

claim: At the highest TBV antibody dose (85%), the TBV alone already reduced parasites in the population to low levels, hence there was insufficient power to detect further synergy.
source: At the highest TBV antibody dose (85%), the TBV alone already reduced parasites in the population to low levels, hence there was insufficient power to detect further synergy between the interventions as all parasites were eliminated from the experimental population (Figure 1).
evidence: Inference from experimental data shown in Figure 1

claim: The presence of TBV antibody (mAb-4B7) reduced oocyst counts in infected mosquitoes (ANOVA: F1,1525 = 75.3, p<0.0001).
source: The presence of TBV antibody (mAb-4B7) reduced oocyst counts in infected mosquitoes (ANOVA: F1,1525 = 75.3, p<0.0001).
evidence: Statistical analysis (ANOVA) of experimental data

claim: TBV antibody presence reduced sporozoite density in infected mosquitoes (ANOVA: F1,707 = 163.9, p<0.0001).
source: Similarly, TBV antibody presence reduced sporozoite density in infected mosquitoes (ANOVA: F1,707 = 163.9, p<0.0001).
evidence: Statistical analysis (ANOVA) of experimental data

claim: At each TBV dose, the tail of the distribution of sporozoites is curtailed progressively across transmission cycles.
source: Figure 3A,B and C further illustrate the effect that TBVs have on sporozoite density distribution for the TBV-50%, 65% and 85% single treatment groups respectively. At each dose, the tail of the distribution of sporozoites is curtailed progressively across transmission cycles.
evidence: Visual representation of experimental data in Figure 3A, B, and C

claim: The efficacy of the PEV is density-dependent, with higher efficacy achieved when mosquitoes have lower sporozoite density.
source: Figure 3D illustrates that the efficacy of the PEV is density-dependent, with higher efficacy achieved when mosquitoes have lower sporozoite density.
evidence: Analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3D

claim: TBV efficacy decreases with increased parasite dose.
source: The efficacy of multiple PEV and TBV candidates against rodent and human parasites have been shown to depend on parasite density; TBV (anti-Pfs25, anti-Pfs48/45 and immune blocking serum) efficacy decreases with increased parasite dose (Churcher et al., 2012; Miura et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citations to Churcher et al., 2012 and Miura et al., 2016

claim: RTS,S only provides sterilizing immunity in volunteers against lightly infected mosquitoes.
source: a representative PEV (RTS,S) only provides sterilizing immunity in volunteers against lightly infected mosquitoes (Churcher et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Churcher et al., 2017

claim: Both PEV and TBV vaccines can halt transmission against a defined quantity of parasites, which is enough to prevent onward infection in lightly infected mosquitoes/humans, but onward transmission is still possible from heavily infected mosquitoes or individuals.
source: This suggests that both types of vaccine can halt transmission against a defined (but currently uncharacterized) quantity of parasites, which is enough to prevent onward infection in lightly infected mosquitoes/humans, but that onward transmission is still possible from heavily infected mosquitoes or individuals.
evidence: Inference from cited studies and experimental observations

claim: A partially effective TBV antibody reduced the number of parasites in infected mosquitoes, ensuring that the PEV antibodies encounter fewer parasites than would otherwise be expected if only a single antibody/vaccine class was administered in isolation.
source: Here, a partially effective TBV antibody reduced the number of parasites in infected mosquitoes, ensuring that the PEV antibodies encounter fewer parasites than would otherwise be expected if only a single antibody/vaccine class was administered in isolation.
evidence: Inference from experimental data

claim: The subsequently reduced parasite burden increased the efficacy of the PEV when co-administered with a TBV.
source: Thus, the subsequently reduced parasite burden increased the efficacy of the PEV when co-administered with a TBV.
evidence: Inference from experimental data

claim: The mechanism behind the observed synergy is the direct result of TBV antibody reducing parasite density in infected mice and thereby enabling the density-dependent PEV antibody to be optimal.
source: this approach is invaluable to demonstrate unequivocally that the mechanism behind the observed synergy is the direct result of TBV antibody reducing parasite density in infected mice and thereby enabling the density-dependent PEV antibody to be optimal (Figure 3).
evidence: Experimental demonstration shown in Figure 3

claim: The mechanism of action of the PEV antibodies administered is matched to the antibody-based mechanism of the RTS,S vaccine.
source: Whilst the murine system uses P. berghei, the mechanism of action of the PEV antibodies administered is matched to the antibody-based mechanism of the RTS,S vaccine; that is sporozoite invasion of the liver is inhibited by the presence of CSP-targeted antibodies in mice both in vivo and ex vivo (Grüner et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Grüner et al., 2003

claim: Sporozoite invasion of the liver is inhibited by the presence of CSP-targeted antibodies in mice both in vivo and ex vivo.
source: that is sporozoite invasion of the liver is inhibited by the presence of CSP-targeted antibodies in mice both in vivo and ex vivo (Grüner et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Grüner et al., 2003

claim: Transmission of human malaria from human-to-mosquito and mosquito-to-human is considered to depend on the density of the parasite.
source: Transmission of human malaria from human-to-mosquito and mosquito-to-human is also considered to depend on the density of the parasite (Churcher et al., 2013; Sinden et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Churcher et al., 2013 and Sinden et al., 2007

claim: The average number of oocysts in wild caught mosquitoes is likely to be substantially lower than the numbers observed in the rodent system.
source: The average number of oocysts in wild caught mosquitoes is likely to be substantially lower than the numbers observed in the rodent system (Rosenberg, 2008)
evidence: Supported by citation to Rosenberg, 2008

claim: Oocyst distribution in wild mosquitoes is highly over-dispersed.

claim: Synergism between PEV and TBVs could potentially enhance the efficacy of the current PEV vaccines, resulting in reduced burden and potentially elimination in areas where it was not previously possible.
source: Synergism between PEV and TBVs could potentially enhance the efficacy of the current PEV vaccines, resulting in reduced burden and potentially elimination in areas where it was not previously possible.

claim: Combining partially effective vaccines of differing anti-parasitic classes may be a pragmatic and powerful way to accelerate malaria elimination efforts.
source: Combining partially effective vaccines of differing anti-parasitic classes may be therefore a pragmatic and powerful way to accelerate malaria elimination efforts.
evidence: Inference from experimental results

claim: mAb-4B7 neutralises the protein Pfs25 in sexual stages of the human malaria P. falciparum and reduces transmission of the parasite from host-to-mosquito.
source: The TBV mAb-4B7 neutralises the protein Pfs25 in sexual stages of the human malaria P. falciparum and reduces transmission of the parasite from host-to-mosquito (Stura et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by citation to Stura et al., 1994

claim: A mAb-4B7 dose of 284.2 µg i.v (244.7-337.3 µg) was required to achieve a reduction in prevalence of 50%.
source: We estimated that a mAb-4B7 dose of 284.2 µg i.v (244.7–337.3 µg) was required to achieve a reduction in prevalence of 50%, a dose of 371.8 µg i.v (319.8–442.8 µg) for 65% reduction and a dose of 629.5 µg i.v (525–777.1 µg) for an 85% reduction.

claim: The anti-P. berghei CSP mAb-3D11 is mechanistically similar to the recently registered RTS,S vaccine for human malaria.
source: The anti-P. berghei CSP mAb-3D11 (Mishra et al., 2012) is mechanistically similar to the recently registered RTS,S vaccine for human malaria, in that the presence of CSP-targeted antibodies in mice inhibit sporozoite invasion of the liver both in vivo and ex vivo (Grüner et al., 2003).

claim: mAb-3D11 antibody was administered at a single sub-optimal dose (50 µg i.v.) that prevented 47.2% (38.0-62.0% 95%CI) of transmission to mice that each received 5 potentially infectious mosquito bites.
